content: The heart is a muscular organ that is responsible for pumping blood through the blood vessels via repeated, rhythmic contractions. This function is also observed in similar structures found in annelids, mollusks, and arthropods. The term cardiac, as used in cardiology, originates from the Greek word kardia, meaning heart. The heart is composed of cardiac muscle, a type of involuntary muscle tissue that is unique to this organ. Over an average human lifespan of 66 years, the heart beats approximately 5 billion times. The human embryonic heart begins to beat around 21 days after conception, which corresponds to about five weeks after the last normal menstrual period (LMP), the standard reference point for dating pregnancy. Initially, the embryonic heart beats at a rate similar to the mother’s, approximately 75–80 beats per minute (BPM). During the first month of beating, the embryonic heart rate (EHR) accelerates linearly, peaking at 165–185 BPM by the early 7th week (or early 9th week after the LMP). This increase occurs at a rate of about 3 BPM per day, or roughly 10 BPM every three days, resulting in a total increase of 100 BPM during the first month. By the 15th week after the LMP, the heart rate decelerates to approximately 152 BPM (±25 BPM). After the 15th week, the deceleration slows, and the average heart rate at term is about 145 BPM (±25 BPM). There is no difference in heart rates between male and female fetuses before birth. In the human body, the heart is typically located in the middle of the thorax, with the largest portion slightly offset to the left. In some cases, such as in dextrocardia, the heart may be situated on the right side. It lies beneath the breastbone and is surrounded by the lungs. The left side of the heart is stronger than the right because it pumps blood to the entire body, which is why the heart is often perceived as being on the left side. The left lung is smaller than the right lung to accommodate the heart's position in the left hemithorax. The heart is enclosed within a sac called the pericardium, which is a double-membrane structure containing serous fluid to reduce friction during heart contractions. The heart resides in the mediastinum, a subdivision of the thoracic cavity. The apex of the heart, its blunt point, is directed inferiorly and to the left. It is located posterior to the 5th intercostal space along the left mid-clavicular line. A stethoscope can be placed over the apex to count heartbeats. In normal adults, the heart weighs between 250–350 grams (9–12 ounces), roughly three-quarters the size of a clenched fist. However, in cases of severe disease, such as hypertrophy, the heart's mass can increase to as much as 1,000 grams (2 pounds). The heart consists of four chambers: two upper atria (singular: atrium) and two lower ventricles. The right side of the heart collects deoxygenated blood in the right atrium from the body and pumps it through the right ventricle into the lungs via the pulmonary circulation. In the lungs, carbon dioxide is exchanged for oxygen through a passive process called diffusion. The left side of the heart collects oxygenated blood from the lungs into the left atrium. From there, the blood moves into the left ventricle, which pumps it out to the rest of the body through the systemic circulation. The ventricles, being the lower chambers, have thicker and stronger walls than the atria. The left ventricle, in particular, has a thicker muscle wall than the right ventricle because it must generate higher force to pump blood through the systemic circulation. Blood flow through the heart begins in the right atrium, where it passes through the tricuspid valve into the right ventricle. From the right ventricle, blood is pumped out through the pulmonary semilunar valve and travels via the pulmonary artery to the lungs. After oxygenation in the lungs, blood returns to the left atrium through the pulmonary veins. It then flows through the bicuspid (mitral) valve into the left ventricle, from which it is pumped out through the aortic semilunar valve into the aorta. The aorta branches into major arteries that supply blood to the upper and lower parts of the body. Blood travels through arteries to smaller arterioles and finally to capillaries, where it delivers oxygen and nutrients to individual cells. Deoxygenated blood then returns through venules, which merge into veins, and eventually flows into the inferior and superior vena cavae, completing the circuit back at the right atrium. The heart functions as a syncytium, a network of interconnected cardiac muscle cells linked by cytoplasmic bridges. This structural arrangement allows electrical stimulation of one cell to spread to neighboring cells, ensuring coordinated contractions. In emergencies involving cardiac arrest (absence of a heartbeat), cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) should be initiated immediately, and emergency medical assistance should be called. If an automated external defibrillator (AED) is available, it can deliver defibrillation if indicated. In most cases, if time permits, the individual should be transported to a hospital for specialized care by a cardiologist, a physician who focuses on the heart and lungs.
